title: The repository is a family of products
summary: Separate the reusable Python harness, terminal application, channel host, protocol adapter, evaluations, and optional providers before tracing an execution.

sections.title: Choose the package for your goal
sections.body:
Start with the product you want to build, not a version number. The same reusable agent can sit behind your Python service, a terminal, a chat channel, or an editor. This Python monorepo packages those responsibilities separately rather than hiding them behind one application's optional-dependencies switch.

Choose your starting package

  • Embed an agent in your own application: use the deepagents SDK (software development kit), whose factory is create_deep_agent.
  • Use the terminal coding application: choose Deep Agents Code, which supplies its own client/server lifecycle and policy.
  • Host conversations in chat channels: study Talon, the experimental long-running host.
  • Connect a graph to an editor: use the Agent Client Protocol (ACP) adapter.
  • Measure model behavior: use the evaluation package and its benchmark integrations.

For an illustrative “read /notes/brief.txt, write /notes/report.txt” request, the SDK composes the agent and tools. A surrounding application still decides how the request arrives, who approves writes, and where the tools execute. Choose that surrounding owner before installing packages.

Translate the choice into an installation and import

A distribution name is what an installer resolves; an import name is what Python loads. The reusable deepagents distribution exports its factory, state, filesystem permissions, delegation types, memory, rubric, and profile registration. The table records this pinned revision, not a promise that all packages share one release cadence.

Directory / distributionImport / executableVersion and Python requirementBoundary
libs/deepagents / deepagentsdeepagents0.7.32; ≥3.11, <4Reusable agent harness.
libs/code / deepagents-codedeepagents_code; dcode, deepagents-code0.2.4; ≥3.14, <3.15Terminal coding application and its server/client policy.
libs/talon / deepagents-talondeepagents_talon; deepagents-talon0.1.0; ≥3.14, <3.15Experimental long-lived channel/scheduling host.
libs/acp / deepagents-acpdeepagents_acp; module entry point0.0.13; ≥3.11, <4Agent Client Protocol adapter.
libs/evals / deepagents-evalsdeepagents_evals, deepagents_harbor; deepagents-evals0.0.1; ≥3.14, <3.15Model-behavior evaluation and benchmark integration.

The deepagents SDK exports composition primitives. Importing that SDK does not launch a terminal, connect a chat channel, or provision a sandbox.

An SDK consumer can remain on Python 3.11 while the current Code application cannot. A checkout containing all packages does not imply one supported interpreter. Follow each package's metadata rather than treating repository-wide prose as a dependency resolver.

sections.title: Applications reuse the harness, but are not interchangeable
sections.body:
Read this dependency map by responsibility, then distinguish checkout development from installed releases. These are independent package relationships, not steps in one launch sequence.

  • Code owns the application stack. Code pins deepagents==0.7.32 exactly and directly depends on LangGraph SDK, CLI, and in-memory runtime packages for its client/server architecture. It also includes Anthropic, Google, and OpenAI integrations, Textual/Rich terminal rendering, FastMCP, and QuickJS.
  • Provider and UI choices are not SDK requirements. These choices belong to the application: they are not a claim that every SDK agent uses Textual or includes all those providers.
  • Talon reuses, then composes. Talon depends on both the SDK and Code. It reuses Code facilities such as model configuration and hooks while building its own host and graph. It is not a hidden terminal window attached to Telegram: DeepAgentRuntime._create_graph calls the SDK directly and adds Talon-specific progress, selection, task, background, and approval middleware.
  • ACP and evaluations choose their construction boundary. ACP accepts either a compiled graph or a context-sensitive graph factory. The evaluation package contains both a pytest behavior harness and an installed Harbor adapter; its benchmark graph can import either SDK construction or Code construction.
  • Editable sources differ from published constraints. Local editable paths in tool.uv.sources make checkout development convenient, but published dependency constraints still matter. Code's local path sources include ACP and the five partner packages. Talon's paths point to SDK and Code.

When diagnosing an unexpected method or version, first establish whether the environment imports the checkout or a published wheel; a directory name is not proof of what Python loaded.

sections.title: Whole-repository coverage without pretending every file is a lesson
sections.body:
The application chapters explain the major runtime contracts and point into implementation and tests. The source atlas complements them for individual functions, provider details, regression tests, scripts, and checked-in assets.

  • Read the coverage claim precisely. “Whole repository” means every package and example family has a place in the map, not that every function has been paraphrased or every test has been executed.
  • Keep the JavaScript repository separate. JavaScript/TypeScript is a separate repository: the root README links to langchain-ai/deepagentsjs. Python QuickJS integration and Talon's JavaScript WhatsApp bridge do not make this checkout the TypeScript SDK implementation.
  • Treat external systems as boundaries. References to Fleet, Harbor, hosted deployment, or external provider SDKs identify boundaries; they do not place those external implementations inside this source tree.

Names are revision-sensitive. The current application is Deep Agents Code, with dcode and deepagents-code scripts. Some example comments and older quickstarts still say deepagents-cli or show deepagents as a command. Read those as historical example text, not as the current installed entrypoint contract.

title: Deep Agents Code: launch to checkpoint
kicker: A terminal client around a server-owned agent
summary: Trace the current coding application from CLI dispatch through graph assembly, local or remote tools, approval interrupts, streaming, and recoverable sessions.

sections.title: Startup selects an execution surface
sections.body:
In normal interactive use, two processes share the work. The terminal process owns Textual rendering and user input. An application-owned LangGraph server process owns the graph and its execution resources. Seeing a proposed tool call in the terminal does not mean the terminal itself executed it.

The client talks to the server over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and receives incremental events through SSE (Server-Sent Events). MCP (Model Context Protocol) sessions connect external tools and belong to the server's event loop. These ownership boundaries explain both configuration delivery and cleanup.

Interactive process lifecycle

  1. Dispatch the requested execution surface. The console scripts resolve to deepagents_code:cli_main. The substantial dispatcher in main.py distinguishes subcommands, ACP (Agent Client Protocol) stdio serving, one-shot non-interactive execution, and interactive Textual execution. These are different policy surfaces, not cosmetic output modes.
  2. Launch the terminal with server arguments. For the normal interactive path, run_textual_cli_async constructs server arguments and launches run_textual_app with backend=None and those arguments.
  3. Construct the graph in the server process. The server's server_graph entry point reads the shared ServerConfig schema that the parent serializes.
  4. Carry settings across the boundary. Changing an in-memory variable in the Textual process does not automatically change the graph; the setting must cross the configuration or run-context boundary.
  5. Report startup failures from the owner. A terminal-rendering error, HTTP/SSE transport failure, provider error, and tool execution error occur in different owners. Server startup emits a machine-readable startup-error marker alongside stderr text.
  6. Clean up on the owning event loop. MCP sessions are bound to the server event loop, so cleanup cannot safely be replaced by an arbitrary late atexit coroutine.
Import-time detail: lazy package attributes

Package-level lazy attribute access avoids eagerly importing startup machinery merely to import deepagents_code. This improves the import boundary; it does not change which process owns the graph after launch.

Ask “which process owned this resource?” before “which widget displayed the error?”

sections.title: create_cli_agent is application composition, not the SDK factory
sections.body:
The SDK factory supplies reusable agent behavior. create_cli_agent wraps that factory with Code's application choices and returns a pair: the compiled agent and the composite backend. HITL means human-in-the-loop: execution can pause for a review decision before a protected tool action runs.

  1. Assemble the application environment. It creates the environment around create_deep_agent: instructions, custom subagents, model retry policy, Git tracing, memory/skills, local context, approvals, hooks, compaction, and optionally rubric, extensions, or interpreter machinery. The final SDK call receives the assembled tools, middleware, backend, CLI context schema, checkpointer, store, and subagent specs.
  2. Create the editable profile when needed. Memory and skills can cause the named agent directory to be created, with an initially empty AGENTS.md marker. This distinguishes the user-editable profile from base coding instructions generated by the application. Memory sources include the user profile instruction file plus discovered project instruction paths.
  3. Keep loading separate from auto-saving. When automatic memory saving is disabled, loading remains enabled but the injected prompt changes; “do not auto-save memory” does not mean “ignore existing instructions.” A guard protects the machine-managed onboarding-name block from agent file edits.
  4. Apply child-graph middleware deliberately. Application middleware is attached to child graphs as well, including server hooks, retry handling, and applicable memory protection.
  5. Install only one approval wrapper. When application-owned HITL middleware is installed, subagent specs receive an explicit empty interrupt_on map so the SDK does not also inherit and install stock HITL. Two independent approval wrappers could otherwise interrupt the same action twice. Middleware identity and assembly order are behavioral contracts.

sections.title: One tool name can cross very different execution boundaries
sections.body:
Code selects a default execution backend, then adds storage-specific routes. Read the two decisions separately.

  1. Choose local shell semantics. With no remote sandbox, Code uses the effective launch directory as its root. Shell-enabled mode chooses LocalShellBackend with virtual_mode=False. The supplied shell environment is already curated, so inherit_env=False avoids reintroducing carrier variables or agent-only tracing credentials.
  2. Choose filesystem-only or remote execution. Without shell access it uses a plain FilesystemBackend. With a remote sandbox it uses the supplied sandbox backend for file and execution operations instead.
  3. Wrap dedicated persistent routes. The default backend is wrapped in CompositeBackend. Local conversation history gets dedicated persistent routing. Large tool results normally use the hardened artifact root, with explicit fallback storage and aliases when that predictable directory is unavailable.
  4. Keep earlier offload paths resolvable. Those aliases remain resolvable so a checkpoint containing an earlier offload path is not invalidated by later recovery.
  5. Validate extension-owned paths. Extension backend routes are validated against protected paths before being merged.
  6. Debug the selected route. To debug a missing file, identify its route first: repository file, persistent conversation archive, large-result offload, or extension-owned path. Looking only in the current working directory can be the wrong investigation.

A local root is not a process security sandbox. This application intentionally gives real host-path semantics to local tools. Tool approval, environment preparation, filesystem routing, and remote isolation solve different problems.

A model instruction saying “work only in this directory” is not equivalent to an operating-system access boundary.

sources.label: Artifact routing, fallback aliases, and extension protection

sections.title: Tokens, tool events, and interrupts are different stream data
sections.body:
The terminal-side RemoteAgent wraps LangGraph's RemoteGraph over HTTP (Hypertext Transfer Protocol) and SSE (Server-Sent Events). Its astream interface yields (namespace, stream_mode, data): where the event came from, what kind it is, and its payload.

  1. Prepare a remote run. It requires a thread ID, prepares mutation ownership, adds the resolved workspace to runtime context, and delegates SSE parsing and namespace negotiation to the upstream client.
  2. Preserve event types. Message dictionaries are converted back to LangChain message objects; update events remain structurally distinct. That separation lets a client render incremental text without confusing it with completed graph state. A token chunk is not proof that a write happened. An updates event carrying an interrupt is not a tool result.
  3. Keep child execution and interrupts distinct. Subgraph namespaces identify child execution, so they must not be flattened indiscriminately into the main assistant answer. The non-interactive stream accumulator likewise separates pending tool-approval interrupts, resume decisions, and hook interrupts.

Illustrative report-edit lifecycle

Suppose a thread has read /notes/brief.txt and an existing draft is at /notes/report.txt. The following is an implementation-derived example, not a recorded model run.

  1. Start the run. The user asks to revise the report from the brief.
  2. Propose the edit. Model messages produce an edit_file call targeting the report; this is intent, not a completed write.
  3. Suspend when required. Hooks and approval routing may pause the graph before the edit executes.
  4. Return the review decision. The client sends a resume decision for the interrupted action.
  5. Execute and observe. Only then can the backend edit execute and return a tool message.
  6. Explain the result. A later model message explains the result; inspect the actual file when confirming the effect.

When a UI looks stuck, distinguish waiting for approval, waiting for a hook response, waiting on the model, and waiting on the execution backend.

sources.label: Hooks wrap tool failures after approval composition

sections.title: A session is more than the currently visible transcript
sections.body:
A session connects three things that must not be confused: discovery metadata, resumable graph state, and external effects. Metadata helps find the right thread and workspace. Checkpoints hold graph state. A write performed by a local or remote backend changes that backend's filesystem, not merely the transcript.

  • Session storage: Code locates a hardened state directory and sessions.db; generated thread IDs are full UUID7 strings. This database is not just a list of session names: the local SQLite saver also stores checkpoint state blobs alongside checkpoint metadata. Thread-list queries can read the smaller metadata without loading every state blob.
  • Connected graph state: the interactive application and remote graph carry checkpointed state, workspace identity, and ownership. A locally seeded remote handoff is a discovery snapshot, not permission to replace the connected server's checkpoints; subsequent history loads from the connected agent.
  • Actual files: a saved checkpoint does not roll back a completed backend write. Nor does a proposed tool call prove that the write occurred.

Illustrative resume after a disconnected display

  1. Before disconnection: the thread reads /notes/brief.txt and starts producing /notes/report.txt. The terminal disconnects before displaying a final result.
  2. On resume: reattach to the same execution context and workspace, rather than replaying the plain text log into a fresh model.
  3. Before repeating the write: inspect checkpoint state and the actual report file. It may already exist even though the terminal never showed completion; alternatively, the action may still have been awaiting approval.

Recovery must coordinate with the server

  1. Cancel before recovery mutation. Transport cancellation does not imply the remote run stopped. RemoteAgent cancels pending/running runs before recovery writes; state updates handle a busy-thread conflict by cancelling and retrying once.
  2. Bound concurrent cancellation waits. Per-run cancellation waits are bounded and concurrent. Escape should not become indefinitely blocked cleanup, but shutdown and an already running side effect can still race.
  3. Inspect durable effects after interruption. Check files and checkpoint state rather than automatically reissuing a write or treating an unfinished stream event as success.

title: Code configuration, trust, and automation
summary: Learn how ranked configuration, model policy, approval modes, MCP, hooks, skills, extensions, and one-shot execution combine without collapsing their security boundaries.

sections.title: Configuration is ranked data with provenance
sections.body:
Configuration resolution answers two questions: “which value wins?” and “why?” Code gives each provider a numeric rank; lower numbers are stronger. A managed policy can therefore override a command-line flag rather than acting only as a fallback.

Resolve a concrete conflict first

Illustrative scalar-resolution example: assume all candidates parse successfully and use managed-model, cli-model, env-model, and fallback-model as teaching labels, not executable model IDs. The same field is supplied at four ranks:

SourceCandidateResult
Managed policy, 200managed-modelSelected.
CLI, 300cli-modelMasked by managed policy.
Environment, 400env-modelMasked by stronger sources.
Default, 1000fallback-modelNot selected.

Remove the managed value and the CLI candidate wins. Remove that too and, with no retained reload or user-TOML candidate, the environment wins. With none of those sources set, the default wins. This example explains precedence; it does not claim any particular model is a shipped default.

The complete resolution contract

  1. Apply all ranked sources. The full order is managed policy 200, CLI 300, retained reload values 350, environment 400, user TOML 500, defaults 1000. Runtime-reload retention is a named tier, not an undocumented environment mutation.
  2. Represent source outcomes explicitly. The resolver is independent of filesystem, model, UI, and manifest details. Providers return typed Found, Unset, or Invalid results: a candidate, an absent value, or a value that could not be accepted. Absence and invalid input are not interchangeable.
  3. Preserve the explanation. A resolved value retains rank-keyed provenance, provider health, diagnostics, selected ranks, and masked ranks. Its constructor rejects inconsistent provenance and freezes copied mappings. A configuration viewer must explain overridden or unhealthy sources as well as the chosen scalar.
  4. Constrain environment loading separately. Project dotenv is untrusted; the configuration module denies selected keys and can bind an immutable construction-scoped environment using a ContextVar. The shell backend receives an explicit prepared copy rather than blindly inheriting the server environment.

If a change seems ignored, distinguish precedence, parsing failure, retained reload values, construction snapshots, and the child-process serialization boundary before editing random environment variables.

sections.title: Model selection includes authorization and retry ownership
sections.body:
create_model supports explicit provider:model strings, inferred bare names, and configured custom model classes.

  1. Parse without misreading provider identifiers. The parser first accounts for configured provider names and Bedrock identifiers that themselves contain a version colon.
  2. Gate the canonical model before side effects. It then computes a canonical spec and calls require_model_allowed before stored credentials are bridged, provider profiles are applied, or provider modules are imported. A model allowlist is therefore an execution-policy gate, not just a UI filter.
  3. Resolve credentials with provider-specific rules. Next come credential resolution and an early missing-credential error for providers where that check is meaningful. Implicit-auth providers are handled differently because absence of an API-key variable does not establish absence of credentials.
  4. Compose parameters and return metadata. Provider defaults/profile data, configured kwargs, and explicit model parameters are composed under application policy. The result contains both the model and metadata used by the application, rather than just a string label.
  5. Keep retry ownership at the model node. Retry ownership is particularly important for latency and billing. Code's factory documents that identifiable provider-owned retry counts are forced off after parameter merging because model-node middleware owns the retry budget. Otherwise a nominal three-attempt application loop could multiply into many hidden SDK attempts.

Unidentifiable custom providers are explicitly a caveat, not magically governed by the same guarantee. When debugging slow failures, inspect both the application retry setting and the actual provider integration.

sources.label: Canonical model selection and policy ordering

sections.title: Manual, Auto, and YOLO are distinct authorization policies
sections.body:
Approval modes decide whether a proposed action needs review before execution. HITL means human-in-the-loop: the graph pauses and waits for a decision. The interactive modes are manual, auto, and yolo; unknown values normalize to Manual.

Start with what each mode does

  • Manual: side-effecting or externally accessing tools are configured for review: execution, writes, edits, deletion, web access, delegation, and relevant MCP (Model Context Protocol) actions. Each review configuration has a runtime predicate, so trusted run-scoped “approve always” state can suppress the interrupt itself.
  • Auto: a specialized HITL replacement evaluates eligible actions using a trusted worktree root, narrow shell allowlist, classifier settings, and trusted tool identities. Auto can deny actions; the classifier validates batch index coverage before binding verdicts to original tool-call IDs.
  • YOLO: the resolved YOLO mode makes the ordinary tool-review predicate return False, so it does not pause for that approval. The construction-level auto_approve option likewise documents automatic shell execution, file writes/edits, web search, and URL fetch. This is approval bypass, not filesystem isolation or a promise that another hook, tool, or provider cannot fail.

Illustrative report write: in Manual, a gated write_file proposal can wait for a person; in Auto, the specialized policy evaluates it; in YOLO, the ordinary approval pause is skipped. None of these choices alone proves /notes/report.txt was written.

Selection and nested-graph rules

  • Expose only eligible modes. The switcher omits Auto when the runtime is ineligible, such as a remote sandbox, and omits YOLO when configured out of the cycle. Leaving an already active YOLO mode remains possible.
  • Separate acknowledgement from display. Warning suppression is cosmetic. Versioned YOLO acknowledgement is tracked separately.
  • Install one approval wrapper per graph. Code prevents children from inheriting a second HITL wrapper. Subagent approval and interpreter bridges require deliberate assembly, not duplicate interrupts.

PTC means programmatic tool calling: interpreter code calls host tools through tools.*. Those calls bypass normal per-tool parent HITL routing. The interpreter's PTC allowlist is a capability boundary, not an optimization toggle. Gating ordinary execute does not necessarily gate the same capability exposed through a bridge.

sections.title: MCP, hooks, skills, and extensions cross different trust boundaries
sections.body:
These extension surfaces grant different kinds of authority. MCP means Model Context Protocol, a protocol for connecting external tools. Read the surfaces as a capability comparison, not as interchangeable plugin mechanisms.

Tools and event automation

  • MCP adds externally implemented tools. The CLI merges discovered configurations with an explicit highest-precedence path, and can disable MCP entirely.
  • Local and remote MCP definitions both require trust. A remote URL or interpolated header can enable SSRF (server-side request forgery) or credential exfiltration even without launching a subprocess. Remembered trust is associated with project and unchanged server definitions; persistent denied names have broader scope. Project trust is not just “is this executable safe?”
  • Hooks are event-driven local automation. Server middleware emits PreCompact, PreToolUse, PostToolUse, PostToolUseFailure, Stop, SubagentStart, and SubagentStop through interrupts for a client runtime to execute and return typed decisions.
  • Hook trust and approval are separate. Project hook handlers can run arbitrary shell commands, so trust is explicit. Hook control flow and ordinary approval interrupts coexist; an unattended runner must resolve the correct kind, not blindly approve every interrupt-shaped payload.

Instructional content and host Python

  • Skills supply instructions and optional associated tooling. The command loader merges built-in, plugin, user profile, user .agents, project .deepagents, project .agents, and experimental Claude sources in ascending precedence.
  • Skill discovery has bounded failure and read scope. Higher-precedence names replace lower ones; one inaccessible source is logged without blocking all discovery. Full-content reads can enforce allowed resolved roots. Skill text is not tool authorization.
  • Extensions execute Python in the host application. The loader imports a module, requires a callable asynchronous extension factory, snapshots registrations, and rolls them back if initialization fails or is cancelled.
  • Registration rollback is not host rollback. Arbitrary Python import side effects are not undone. Backend route validation protects app-owned storage names, but trusted Python can still perform host operations. This is a stronger trust grant than reading a Markdown skill.

sections.title: Headless execution is not interactive Auto without a screen
sections.body:
Headless execution has no person at a terminal to resolve arbitrary approval prompts. The one-shot runner therefore derives a separate shell policy; interactive Auto/YOLO flags do not turn it into “Auto without a screen.” HITL means human-in-the-loop review, and MCP means Model Context Protocol external-tool integration.

Choose the shell capability explicitly

  • No commands: an empty or absent allowlist disables shell access.
  • Named commands: a restrictive list such as ["cat", "grep"] checks command names and dangerous shell patterns.
  • Unrestricted: --shell-allow-list=all parses to the special SHELL_ALLOW_ALL sentinel. A sentinel is a distinguished value with its own type, not an executable named “all.” It bypasses the restrictive pattern/token checks for nonempty commands.

Illustrative restrictive-policy decisions

With only cat and grep allowed, cat /notes/brief.txt passes the shell matcher. rm /notes/report.txt fails because rm is not listed. cat /notes/brief.txt > /notes/report.txt fails the dangerous-pattern check even though its first command is allowed.

A pipeline also needs every command segment allowed: cat /notes/brief.txt | grep summary can pass, while adding an unlisted wc cannot. These are source-derived policy examples, not executed commands or a full operating-system sandbox.

Shell matching is not read-only mode. Without configured permission hooks, exposed non-shell tools ordinarily run without human approval. Rejecting shell redirection does not prevent an exposed write_file from writing /notes/report.txt, subject to that tool's own permissions and backend. Shell matching, filesystem-tool exposure, permission hooks, and the headless MCP guard are separate controls.

One-shot execution and machine outcomes

  1. Resolve execution settings. They come from the shell policy, not the interactive switch. Permission hooks can change how the interrupt path is configured.
  2. Apply headless gates. The CLI warns that explicit interactive Auto/YOLO flags have no effect here. Shell access follows --shell-allow-list; MCP routing is fail-closed, including a headless guard for gated MCP tool names.
  3. Interpret the exit. The runner returns 130 for interruption, 124 for the bounded HITL/turn-budget failure path, 1 for execution/resume failures, and 0 on ordinary completion or deliberate client-hook stop.
  4. Check the artifact. Zero exit does not universally prove the user's business objective. Combine status with the requested artifact or explicit acceptance checks.
GitHub action wrapper: arguments, timeout, and untrusted output

The composite action builds an argument array, validates JSON and Boolean inputs, runs dcode --non-interactive or a stdin path under an outer timeout, and captures the first pipeline stage's status rather than tee's. It uses a random delimiter when writing untrusted model output to GitHub outputs and rejects stdin plus skill in its own wrapper.

Workflow permissions, secrets, shell allowlist, project trust, and memory-cache scope remain operator decisions. The action does not make repository content trusted instructions.

title: Talon: a long-running channel host
kicker: Events, authority, history, and scheduled work
summary: Follow chat messages and scheduled prompts through a host that owns channel lifetimes, conversation replacement, protected approvals, background results, and multiple persistence layers.

sections.title: The process host and the agent graph are separate owners
sections.body:
Talon keeps an agent available across channel events instead of launching a new terminal for each message. The host owns chat connections and scheduled delivery; the runtime invokes the agent graph. Talon is explicitly experimental, so those useful boundaries should not be mistaken for a production-service guarantee.

Model-backed startup

  1. Select adapters and prepare local state. The executable reads TalonConfig, prepares assistant-local state and cron storage, constructs enabled WhatsApp, Telegram, Discord, and Slack adapters, and enters the host. Channel flags and corresponding environment switches select adapters.
  2. Open execution and persistence resources. The model-backed path opens an optional sandbox, then the configured checkpointer and independent history archive. It wraps the stores in ConversationSaver, loads MCP (Model Context Protocol) tools, and constructs DeepAgentRuntime.
  3. Compose the graph directly with the SDK. It calls create_deep_agent, adding filesystem handling with binary offload outside StateBackend, selected-model summarization, model selection, progress messages, HITL (human-in-the-loop review), server hooks, task selection, background middleware, skills, memory, and the checkpointer.
  4. Enter the host lifecycle. The host manages channel and scheduler lifetimes while the runtime owns invocation. Without a channel, the default assembly does not create the channel-delivery scheduler.
No-model startup and lifecycle-only runs

When no model is configured, _agent_runtime returns EchoAgentRuntime. Do not infer “always runs an LLM” from the stale main-function docstring. A run-once start/stop exercises component lifecycle, not a successful real channel conversation.

This is a local runtime host, not a distributed task queue or hosted Fleet service.

sources.label: Host, sandbox, archive, and scheduler wiring

sections.title: An end-to-end message trace: chat identity to delivered reply
sections.body:
Consider an illustrative authorized Slack request: “read /notes/brief.txt and produce /notes/report.txt.” Talon must keep both the conversation's identity and the current reply's ownership straight. It uses two counters with different jobs, not one generic “generation.”

  • Conversation-reset generation: a persisted counter maps a channel conversation root to the current agent thread. Starting a new conversation changes this mapping so later messages use a different graph thread.
  • Active-turn generation: an in-process counter identifies which asynchronous turn may still deliver a reply. Replacing active work invalidates older results without, by itself, resetting the conversation's checkpoint identity.

Message-to-result lifecycle

  1. Normalize and dispatch. The adapter converts the provider event into a ChannelMessage and dispatches through its handler.
  2. Resolve and serialize routing. Provider identity plus channel conversation ID becomes a conversation root. A history-scope lock and a conversation lock serialize routing decisions.
  3. Intercept control messages. Commands, pending tool approvals, and pending authorization callbacks are handled before ordinary text reaches the agent.
  4. Select the graph thread. The root plus the persisted conversation-reset generation resolves the agent conversation ID.
  5. Replace active work safely. An already running turn is cancelled and repaired. If cancellation times out, the host refuses overlapping work and sends its cancellation-timeout message.
  6. Assign active-turn ownership. The host increments the active-turn generation and launches a named task with model/effort selections and route metadata.
  7. Bind trusted callbacks. Progress delivery, approval, and OAuth (authorization) handlers are supplied separately from inbound metadata. A typing refresh task runs alongside the turn.
  8. Settle and deliver. After an AgentResult, the host stops typing, clears authorization state, verifies both current thread identity and active-turn generation, delivers the result, and records the text actually delivered.

Illustrative second-message and reset trace

  1. First request: thread A has an active report-writing turn. Its reply is associated with its captured active-turn generation.
  2. Second ordinary message: “make it shorter” replaces active work, subject to cancellation succeeding. The conversation-reset mapping still selects thread A, but a newer active-turn generation owns delivery. An obsolete first reply is dropped rather than delivered late.
  3. Explicit new conversation: after cancelling old work, the host persists a bumped reset counter. The next ordinary message resolves to thread B. That changes conversation context, not just which pending reply wins.

If an obsolete result consumed background results without reporting them, those results are requeued. The trace is source-derived, not a recorded channel exchange; replacing a turn also does not imply completed filesystem effects were undone.

A lock protects a brief routing decision. The active-turn generation guards a result that may arrive much later; the reset generation selects the durable conversation thread. Each protects a different lifetime.

sections.title: Being allowed to send a message is not approval authority
sections.body:
Shared channel exposure has three modes: self, allowlist, and open.

  1. Apply channel admission policy. Self checks the adapter's operator/self identity; allowlist matches configured conversations or mention patterns; open permits arbitrary senders only after an explicit risk acknowledgement. These are application admission controls, not identity guarantees supplied by the model.
  2. Derive approval authority from trusted configuration. Tool approval authority is narrower than admission. The host computes an operator Boolean from trusted channel configuration and passes it separately into _invoke_agent. That method overwrites the metadata value and forces it false for cron or background-delivery turns. Untrusted incoming metadata cannot grant itself operator status.
  3. Bind decisions to the original requester. Approval requests retain provider, chat, originating sender, action count, and prompt identity. Text replies from another sender are rejected; reaction decisions undergo additional matching before resolving the pending future.
  4. Keep OAuth outside model context. MCP OAuth is another host-owned flow. Authorization URL/device-code events are designed to bypass model context.
  5. Validate the pending callback identity. A pasted callback is intercepted before it reaches the model, checked against pending provider/chat/sender identity, checked for expiry, and parsed against the bound redirect URI. A plausible URL in an unrelated chat is not enough to complete the flow.
  6. End authorization with the owning turn. Background workers explicitly remove the authorization handler so an OAuth prompt cannot outlive the host turn that was supposed to clean it up.

The warning states the central risk plainly: those senders can trigger an agent operating with operator credentials and local host access.

sources.label: Auth events stay outside model context

sections.title: Checkpoint, searchable history, and live jobs are different stores
sections.body:
Ask whether you want to continue execution or find past conversation evidence. A checkpoint answers the first question: it restores the graph's resumable state. A history archive answers the second: it stores conversation-oriented records and can support retrieval. Searching old messages does not itself resume the thread that produced them.

Illustratively, “continue the report we were editing” needs the right graph thread and checkpoint. “Find last month's discussion of this brief” is an archive/search task. A report file is a third concern: neither a search result nor a checkpoint alone establishes the current contents of /notes/report.txt.

Storage responsibilities

  • Checkpoints: resumable graph state.
  • Archive: conversation records, namespaced by assistant, with optional vector retrieval.
  • Live jobs: in-process background workers, not durable restartable executions.
Backend selection, archive coordination, and search visibility

The host opens checkpoint and history backends independently. Both default to local SQLite paths, and each can select a URI scheme. Checkpoints support SQLite/file, PostgreSQL, MongoDB variants, and a scheme-specific installed entry point when exactly one matches.

Remote archive drivers and embedding providers are optional dependencies, not silently available infrastructure. ConversationSaver wraps the checkpointer and archive without owning either lifetime. It delegates checkpoint reads and serialization permissions, and protects active sessions against deletion through conversation tools.

Synchronous writes and administrative copy/prune paths are deliberately unsupported so they cannot bypass archival behavior. Coordination by one wrapper does not make two independent stores a database transaction.

History visibility is backend-specific. Construction marks MongoDB search visibility as unknown and other supported selections as immediate. Atlas server-side embeddings require MongoDB history. Vector-generation preparation and embedding profile setup are explicit initialization stages.

A missing search hit may involve archive scope, embedding generation, or index visibility rather than a missing checkpoint. Conversely, clearing visible chat context does not prove archives, vector records, media, hook transcripts, and provider caches were removed.

A durable checkpoint and a persisted cron definition do not make an in-flight Python background task restartable. The worker registry is explicitly memory-only. Plan operational recovery around those separate lifetimes.

sources.label: Archive wrapper ownership and active protection

sections.title: Detached subagents have delivery and acknowledgement semantics
sections.body:
Talon's background middleware intercepts the existing SDK task and remote start_async_task surfaces; it does not replace the child's compiled graph with an unrelated worker implementation.

In-process background lifecycle

  1. Register and launch under shared limits. For an ordinary conversation it requires a thread owner, prunes settled jobs, enforces registry/running ceilings under a shared lock, allocates a task ID, copies context, launches an asyncio task, and returns an immediate started message. Nested remote delegation from a subagent is refused.
  2. Bind the worker thread and reduced authority. The worker switches to its own task thread and recursion limit, clears approval-operator authority, removes the authorization handler, and retains needed history/cron scope.
  3. Bound execution, results, and errors. It is time-bounded; results are capped, and exceptions become bounded failure messages rather than raw credential-bearing errors. A child graph that reaches approval cannot silently run the protected action: a returned interrupt is represented as “needs tool approval” data.
  4. Deliver results as labelled data. Completed results remain pending for their owning main conversation. They are injected as labelled subagent-result data, not a new top-level trusted user command.
  5. Acknowledge only a completed main turn. Acknowledgement happens only after the main agent completes a turn. If host delivery loses a race or is cancelled, it can requeue consumed results.

This is closer to an in-process acknowledgement protocol than a simple fire-and-forget task list. Nevertheless, the registry itself is not persisted and is not an exactly-once distributed message system.

sources.label: Interception, ownership, capacity, and task creation
Worker context, deadlines, interrupts, and bounded results
Delivery race returns results to pending work

sections.title: Scheduling claims a run before executing it
sections.body:
PersistentCronScheduler scans on a configurable interval whose default is 60 seconds.

Scheduled invocation lifecycle

  1. Scan and claim due work. A tick first discards finished jobs, gets due jobs, and executes them sequentially within that tick. Before running a job it calls advance_next_run; if the store does not return a claim, it does not run. This ordering prevents the scheduler from merely rediscovering an unchanged due record while an invocation is underway.
  2. Create a bounded, fresh graph thread. Each scheduled invocation gets a fresh job-derived graph thread with a random suffix. It is bounded by a host timeout and attempts interruption recovery on expiry.
  3. Bind read-only context without live approval authority. When the origin channel is unambiguous, it can receive the origin chat's read-only history scope. It does not receive a live operator approval or OAuth callback.
  4. Await delegation within the scheduled turn. Scheduled delegation is awaited inline instead of detached because there is no later chat delivery turn to collect a result.
  5. Record completion, then decide delivery. Success and delivery are tracked separately. The scheduler records the model run, suppresses output beginning or ending with [SILENT], and otherwise calls the delivery callback.
  6. Handle delivery and scan failures separately. A delivery exception changes the recorded job status to error even though the agent may already have completed work. The scan loop catches ordinary exceptions, logs them, waits the normal interval, and continues rather than spinning or dying silently.

The claim-before-execute sequence also means this code should not be described as crash-proof exactly-once scheduling: this inspected path does not replay a run atomically with external side effects.

For debugging, separate “was due,” “was claimed,” “agent completed,” “silent,” and “channel delivered.”

sources.label: Claim, outcome, silence, and delivery status
Fresh scheduled thread and history scope

title: ACP: graph execution as an editor protocol
kicker: Handshake, sessions, streams, and permission requests
summary: Understand what the Agent Client Protocol adapter translates, what remains the graph factory’s responsibility, and why durable sessions and exact-command approval are explicit features.

sections.title: The adapter is a protocol boundary, not a second agent harness
sections.body:
ACP means Agent Client Protocol. Think of its adapter as a translator between an editor and an existing agent graph: editor requests become graph operations; graph messages, plans, tools, and permission pauses become editor updates. The graph still supplies agent behavior, and the application still supplies execution policy.

For an illustrative report request, the editor sends a prompt, the graph proposes reading the brief or writing the report, and the adapter streams progress back. If the graph pauses for approval, the adapter asks the editor for a decision and resumes that pause. It is not a second harness deciding how the agent should solve the task.

Supply the graph before choosing the protocol features

AgentServerACP subclasses the ACP agent interface. It accepts either a compiled graph or a synchronous factory taking AgentSessionContext(cwd, mode, model): the session working directory and its selected mode/model.

  • Fixed graph or reconstructable factory: mode and model catalogs require a factory because a fixed graph cannot be rebuilt for changed selections. The server retains working directories, mode/model choices, plans, cancellation flags, MCP (Model Context Protocol) declarations, and permission caches.
  • Advertised capabilities: initialization returns the protocol version and capabilities. Image prompting is advertised; durable loading is advertised only when the constructor enables it.
  • Application responsibilities: the adapter does not independently provision a secure backend, define all tool policy, or make arbitrary model choices safe. The supplied factory and application own those choices.

Choose the intended serving assembly

The bare python -m deepagents_acp entry calls a test-agent serving function. Code's dcode --acp is a different assembly: it loads Code model/tools/configuration, builds through a per-session factory, enables loading, and serves over stdio using the ACP dependency's runner.

Code additionally supplies thread leases and, for Auto, trusted control-state handling. These are not automatic features of every user-created ACP server. The following sections distinguish durable checkpoint state from process-local conversation state and then trace the permission round trip.

sources.label: Code graph factory, leases, and ACP serving

sections.title: Session creation and durable loading are not the same operation
sections.body:
Session creation, durable loading, and in-process conversation memory are different contracts.

  1. Create and optionally persist the session. A new session gets a random hexadecimal UUID, stores its working directory and MCP declarations, initializes options, and optionally persists empty state plus ACP metadata.
  2. Require durable checkpoint storage for loading. A session configured for durable loading requires a real checkpointer.
  3. Validate and restore the original session. During load, the adapter retrieves checkpoint metadata, requires an ACP-session marker, and rejects a working directory that differs from the one used at creation. It restores options and replays human, AI, and tool messages back to the client.
  4. Use process-local fallback only for ordinary prompts. In contrast, ordinary prompt processing adds a MemorySaver when the supplied graph lacks a checkpointer. This supports conversation state on the current graph instance, but it cannot satisfy restart persistence.
  5. Opt into restart persistence explicitly. Advertising session/load is therefore a separate opt-in contract. A process-local map of session IDs is not enough; the checkpoint backend and durable metadata must survive.
  6. Reuse checkpoint storage across rebuilds. The session ID remains the graph thread identity, but the factory can return a new graph. History is available only if that graph reconnects to the same checkpoint storage. A fresh MemorySaver under the same thread ID has no old checkpoints; the automatic fallback does not guarantee continuity across session, model, or mode rebuilds.

Do not interpret this source as a blanket concurrency guarantee for arbitrary overlapping client prompts: the adapter retains one active graph instance and active-session marker while maintaining multiple session maps. Integrators should inspect their transport's request scheduling rather than assuming a stateless HTTP-handler model.

sources.label: Session config and required durable checkpointer
Session factory reset and in-process fallback

sections.title: Prompt execution loops across graph interrupts
sections.body:
The adapter converts ACP text, image, audio, resource, and embedded-resource variants through dedicated conversion helpers before constructing LangChain messages.

Conversion and prompt lifecycle

  1. Convert only the implemented payloads. Actual support is narrower than the union of accepted schema types: text is copied, inline images become data URLs, resource references are rendered as descriptive text, and audio conversion explicitly raises NotImplementedError.
  2. Stream messages and graph updates. The graph stream requests messages and updates with subgraphs enabled.
  3. Translate streamed tool and plan state. Tool-call chunks are accumulated for protocol tool updates, todo changes become plan updates, and interrupt updates suspend ordinary execution.
  4. Resume the interrupt rather than resubmit input. The outer loop then obtains decisions and resumes using Command(resume={"decisions": ...}) rather than appending the original user prompt again. This distinction prevents approval round-trips from becoming duplicate conversational inputs.
  5. Observe cooperative cancellation. Cancellation is represented as a session flag checked before and during streaming; the prompt response reports cancelled when observed, otherwise end_turn on completion.

A resource URI is not automatically read from disk by the conversion helper, and making its display path relative is not an access-control check.

This is cooperative control observed by the adapter, not a promise that every external side effect has been rolled back. A client should show the difference between an interrupted turn and a failed tool result, and should not retry execution based solely on a disconnected display.

sources.label: Content conversion, stream, cancellation, and resume loop
Actual conversion behavior and unsupported audio

sections.title: Always allow execute means an exact request in an exact context
sections.body:
Read the permission round-trip first, then its two different reuse contracts.

Approval lifecycle

  1. Request a decision for interrupted actions. When a graph interrupts, the adapter extracts action requests and sends ACP request_permission messages with approve, reject, and conditionally always-allow options.
  2. Resolve unknown or cancelled decisions safely. Unknown selected option IDs normalize to rejection; a cancelled permission request is rejection.
  3. Update approved plans separately. Approved todo plans have special in-progress update handling, separate from execution approval.

Permission reuse contracts

  1. Key execution grants by the complete request. For execute, reusable permission is keyed by AgentSessionContext and canonical JSON of the entire argument dictionary.
  2. Validate arguments before canonicalization. The request must contain a nonempty string command and be losslessly JSON serializable with non-finite values disallowed. Sorting object keys avoids treating mere dictionary order as a different request.
  3. Ask again when arguments or context change. Changing command text, timeout, working-directory arguments, environment arguments, selected mode/model, or session working directory changes the key.
  4. Do not generalize execute semantics to other tools. Non-execute tools use a broader per-tool-name session cache instead, so the security semantics are intentionally not identical.
  5. Read regression coverage for intended distinctions. The regression tests demonstrate the intended distinctions directly: a changed command asks again, an identical request reuses permission, changed arguments or context ask again, and another session cannot reuse the grant.

These tests are source evidence of the contract, not a claim that they were run for this learning site. The adapter's exact-request policy should also not be conflated with helper functions that parse command types for other allowlist purposes.

sources.label: Request, context, and session isolation regression assertions

title: Partners and examples: choose a composition pattern
summary: Inventory all partner distributions and example families, then distinguish sandbox adapters, interpreter capabilities, instructional profiles, outer loops, and genuinely different application architectures.

sections.title: Five partner packages, two fundamentally different roles
sections.body:
Choose an example for the boundary you want to learn: constructing an agent, changing where its tools run, or adding an outer control loop. Examples are compositions to inspect and adapt, not a single recommended production architecture.

A recommended first reading path

  1. Begin with deep_research. Follow its compact create_deep_agent call: model, tools, instructions, and researcher child. This exposes the core composition without the terminal application's process lifecycle.
  2. Choose a second example by goal. Study content-builder-agent for file-backed instructions and skills, text-to-sql-agent for a toolkit, or nvidia_deep_agent for multiple models and remote GPU/CPU execution.
  3. Add infrastructure only when it answers your question. Compare sandbox providers if tools must run remotely; inspect QuickJS for interpreter-driven tool calls. Choose Ralph, rubric, better-harness, wiki, or the async server when the outer workflow is what you need to understand.

That is a reading recommendation, not evidence these examples have run here. Model credentials, service access, database files, and example-local dependencies remain prerequisites.

Five partner packages, two roles

Four packages adapt remote execution/file APIs to the SDK backend protocol. QuickJS instead adds an interpreter tool and lifecycle through middleware. A backend and interpreter can coexist; selecting one does not select the other. All five distributions declare Python >=3.11,<4.0.

sections.title: Backend compatibility does not erase provider semantics
sections.body:
The normal execution story is simple: submit a command to the selected provider, wait for completion, and return its output and exit status. A timeout bounds waiting or execution according to that provider's adapter; it is not evidence that every remote process was stopped or that prior file effects were undone.

Illustratively, cat /notes/brief.txt can finish before the deadline and return text plus a successful exit status. If a different command exceeds its deadline, inspect both the reported status and provider cleanup behavior before retrying. This is a conceptual trace, not a provider run.

Provider-specific execution and resource contracts

ProviderExecution or resource lifecycleImportant boundary or caveat
ModalCalls bash -c, waits, reads stdout/stderr, and returns the provider exit code.Binary file helpers reject non-absolute paths and map filesystem errors.
DaytonaUses session commands/logs with one remaining-deadline budget across requests and a small best-effort cleanup allowance.Compensates for provider timeout rounding and an added SDK HTTP timeout buffer. These are material differences beneath the shared execute interface.
VercelLaunches a detached bash -lc command, waits against the effective deadline, attempts to kill timed-out work, and reports timeout code 124.

A failed kill is logged because the command can remain alive and incur cost.

If log fetching fails after completion, the exit code is preserved and unavailable output is reported rather than erasing the completed outcome.

The output cap uses string slicing although the constant/message call it bytes; it is not byte-precise UTF-8 accounting.

RunloopCan attach a devbox or select/create a blueprint. It paginates exact-name discovery, accepts completed builds, distinguishes failed from still-building states, and avoids duplicating a same-name incomplete blueprint.The constructor's timeout parameter is reserved for API parity rather than consumed as a creation deadline.

A shared method name does not erase provider semantics. For diagnostics, inspect provider-specific timeout, process cleanup, file, lifecycle, and snapshot behavior.

sources.label: Vercel detached execution, cleanup, and output handling
Blueprint pagination and build state handling

sections.title: Interpreter safety depends on bridges, not just VM isolation
sections.body:
QuickJS is an embedded JavaScript engine. Here, middleware exposes a REPL (read–evaluate–print loop) tool inside the Python agent process; it is not a remote cloud machine. Each LangGraph thread gets a private interpreter slot, with thread-, turn-, or call-scoped persistence.

The direct VM (virtual machine) schema promises no filesystem, network, or real-clock access. External capabilities arrive through explicitly enabled host bridges. PTC means programmatic tool calling: JavaScript invokes Python tools through tools.*, so bridge configuration determines what the interpreter can actually do.

Separate the resource and authority budgets

  • Memory and output: source defaults include a 64 MiB heap allowance and independently bounded result/stdout text. These are separate from execution time and tool-call limits.
  • Execution time: the default five-second budget measures VM execution, excluding time spent waiting for Python tools.* coroutines. A slow host call can exceed five seconds of wall time without exhausting VM time.
  • Host-call count: the default PTC budget is 256 bridge calls. Limiting count does not establish whether a tool is authorized; exposure and approval are separate decisions.
  • Delegation: JavaScript task(...) runs inside an approved interpreter invocation and does not trigger parent HITL (human-in-the-loop review) for every dispatch. Gate the interpreter, constrain exposed tools, add child-graph approval, or disable that dispatch path as appropriate.

What persisted interpreter state means

State has a private slot identifier, snapshot payload, and HMAC channel. HMAC means hash-based message authentication code: a keyed integrity tag, not encryption. When a snapshot signing key is configured in thread mode, snapshots are signed before checkpointing and verified before restore; missing or mismatched tags are rejected.

Without a signing key, persisted snapshots are not integrity-checked. This is a storage-trust concern separate from whether JavaScript can call an external tool. “Sandboxed JavaScript” needs both the VM restrictions and the actual bridge policy explained.

Disabling timeout is hazardous: asyncio cancellation cannot stop a runaway VM evaluation. Disabling the PTC call budget permits unbounded bridge-call loops. External admission and deadline controls are still needed for untrusted workloads.

Per-thread isolation, timeout limits, host calls, and child dispatch

sections.title: Direct SDK examples: research, content, SQL, and GPU work
sections.body:
These examples all construct agents directly, but vary the supplied tools, instructions, subagents, and execution backend. Read one complete example at a time rather than treating the collection as a launch sequence.

deep_research — instructions and specialist delegation

This example constructs an SDK agent with an Anthropic model, Tavily/think tools, a research system prompt, and a researcher subagent. It is a useful first composition to inspect because the top-level factory call makes those inputs visible. It does not include the full Code terminal runtime.

content-builder-agent — file-backed profiles and an example-local loader

It loads memory and skills from files, adds image-generation tools, and converts a YAML mapping keyed by subagent name into a list of subagent specifications through its own loader. That helper does not mean the core SDK natively discovers arbitrary YAML subagents.

text-to-sql-agent — database toolkit authority

It builds a SQLDatabaseToolkit against its configured database, supplies those tools plus instruction/skill files, uses a local FilesystemBackend, and explicitly supplies an empty subagent list. Database/toolkit authorization still matters: a text-to-SQL use case does not make an arbitrary database connection read-only.

nvidia_deep_agent — multiple models and remote processing

A configurable frontier orchestrator delegates to NVIDIA Nemotron research and a separate data-processing child. Its actual backend factory returns a ModalSandbox, selects GPU or CPU from runtime context, attaches a named sandbox or creates one, and seeds skill/memory files only on creation.

NVIDIA's introductory module prose mentions CompositeBackend routing, but the inspected factory does not construct one. Memory edits persist for the sandbox lifetime, not in a durable external memory service. This illustrates why implementation is stronger evidence than introductory comments.

sources.label: Example-local YAML loader and SDK composition
Actual Modal factory and one-time seed

sections.title: Outer-loop examples solve a different orchestration problem
sections.body:
An outer loop decides when to call an agent again, how to evaluate its work, or where to deliver it. That is different from the tool/model loop inside one graph invocation. Each example below owns a distinct outer-loop contract.

ralph_mode — repeat against the working filesystem

Ralph repeatedly calls Code's run_non_interactive, prompting the next iteration to inspect prior filesystem work. A limit of zero is unbounded; exit 130 breaks, while other nonzero exits are printed and the loop continues.

There is no independent objective-success detector in this loop. Persistence is largely the working filesystem. An unlimited default is not an efficiency or convergence guarantee: repeated runs can inspect the same report artifact without proving it meets the user's objective.

rubric_middleware — bounded drafting and grading

A drafting agent, grader, and acceptance rubric form a feedback loop with an iteration bound and LangSmith-oriented real-model configuration. Unlike mere repetition, this example gives the loop an explicit judgment surface.

better-harness — optimize editable harness surfaces

This optimization workspace materializes editable surfaces under /current, exposes train feedback/history, invokes a proposer, reloads changes, and builds a candidate variant. Improvement on visible training cases is not by itself evidence of generalization.

llm-wiki — analyze, then conditionally file

The query workflow first requests read-only analysis and an explicit filing decision. A missing decision defaults to skip; the decision is logged, and a separate filing pass runs only when selected. Its instructions distinguish canonical wiki evidence from operational logs and previous query-routing hints.

async-subagent-server — coordinate a remote researcher

A supervisor graph pairs with a remote researcher target. This demonstrates SDK remote subagent coordination, not Talon's process-local background registry.

These are application-level orchestration choices around the harness. None is a universal behavior silently supplied by every SDK agent.

sources.label: Actual autonomous outer loop and exit behavior
Evidence prompt and fail-closed filing parser

sections.title: Deployment and profile examples are assets, not bundled hosting implementations
sections.body:
The remaining families mainly package configuration and profile assets. They show what to hand to a runtime or deployment platform, not an implementation of that external platform.

Four deployment-manifest examples

  • deploy-coding-agent supplies a named agent.json deployment manifest.
  • deploy-content-writer supplies its own named manifest and content-oriented profile assets.
  • deploy-gtm-agent adds a description identifying research/content coordination.
  • deploy-mcp-docs-agent supplies its own named manifest for the docs-agent role.

All four contain runtime model identifiers. Their instruction, skill, and subagent assets describe intended roles, but a six-line manifest is not the hosting implementation. Model IDs are example-specific choices at this revision, not package defaults.

downloading_agents — a portable profile layout

This family packages a content-writer archive with AGENTS.md and skill directories. Its README still pins deepagents-cli==0.0.13 and the old executable. Reuse the folder/profile idea without treating those old startup commands as current Code instructions.

talon — a container assembly

The container example's final command runs deepagents-talon, with workspace and MCP configuration environment setup.

These six directories plus research, content-builder, SQL, NVIDIA, Ralph, rubric, better-harness, wiki, and async-server account for all fifteen top-level example directories in this checkout.

This is a source map, not evidence that credentials, remote services, database files, deployment permissions, or provider models were available or that the examples ran here. Inspect implementation and local metadata before production reuse.

title: Evaluations: inspect what the score actually measures
kicker: Behavioral tests, trajectories, trials, and external datasets
summary: Separate deterministic regression tests from real-model evaluations and benchmark adapters; understand why passing correctness does not imply optimal tool use or production safety.

sections.title: Real-model evaluations are an explicit operating mode
sections.body:
Decide what you want to measure before choosing a command. An offline regression, a model-behavior probe, repeated trials, and a benchmark adapter answer different questions. None substitutes for all the others.

Match evidence to its purpose

Evidence surfaceQuestion it helps answerWhat it does not establish alone
Offline harness unit testsDoes deterministic harness logic meet its tested contracts?A real model's task success.
Real-model evaluation casesDid this model/harness configuration meet these task assertions?Universal success or production safety.
Repeated trials and aggregationHow variable are the measured outcomes?Validity of uninspected assertions or all deployments.
External benchmark adaptersHow does the chosen graph perform under that dataset, environment, and verifier contract?Equivalence to a differently configured runner.

Selection tiers are not scoring rules

baseline and hillclimb are test-selection tier tags. Category filters select subject matter. Neither is the same distinction as hard correctness versus soft efficiency: .success(...) can fail a selected case, while .expect(...) logs trajectory/efficiency feedback without failing it.

For example, selecting a tier changes which cases run. Requiring the final report file to contain particular content changes a case's pass condition. Expecting one read instead of three changes efficiency feedback. Keep those three decisions separate when interpreting a score.

Prepare and select the real-model run

  1. Satisfy prerequisites. libs/evals/tests/evals is not another offline unit-test folder. Its conftest aborts without tracing and requires an explicit --model.
  2. Select supported paths. The suite registers categories and baseline/hillclimb tiers, supports category inclusion/exclusion, and rejects unknown filter values. Marked tests may run through QuickJS; --repl quickjs skips unsupported or unmarked tests rather than making every test interpreter-compatible.
  3. Map categories to scenarios. The registry covers file operations, retrieval, tool use, memory, conversation, summarization, unit-test feedback, and LangChain middleware. Concrete files cover skills, subagents, todos, cross-turn memory, context summarization, goal tools, follow-up quality, Auto authorization, constrained/relational tool use, and external benchmarks.
  4. Record the full configuration. Keep the explicit model spec, provider routing/fallback policy, reasoning settings, interpreter selection, harness revision, tier/category selection, and trial count.
  5. Record routing, not just a model name. Strict OpenRouter provider-selection and reasoning-effort flags exist because settings affect measured behavior. One endpoint's result cannot be casually attributed to every endpoint serving a similarly named model.

These are curated capability and regression probes, not a complete specification of everything the application can do. The next sections explain trajectories, report aggregation, and the benchmark catalog in that order.

sources.label: Tracing and explicit model are mandatory
Eval filters, routing, reasoning, and REPL flags

sections.title: Correctness assertions fail; efficiency expectations only log
sections.body:
A trajectory is the agent's route through a task: actions, tool observations, and resulting files, not only its final prose. run_agent converts graph results into AgentTrajectory so tests can inspect that route as well as the answer.

Invocation and trajectory lifecycle

  1. Prepare the invocation. run_agent builds inputs, allocates a thread ID when absent, and logs model/run inputs.
  2. Invoke and normalize. It calls the compiled graph, logs outputs, checks for a mapping result, and converts it into an AgentTrajectory.
  3. Retain evidence. Ordered AI actions and corresponding tool observations sit alongside a normalized file map. This preserves how the answer was obtained.

Two scoring contracts, independent of selection tier

Scorer APIEffect
.success(...)Hard correctness assertions: violations fail the case.
.expect(...)Soft efficiency/trajectory expectations: feedback is logged but never fails the case.

The implementation logs actual step/tool-call counts, evaluates expectation feedback, then calls pytest.fail only for violated success assertions. A green test can therefore have an inefficient or unexpected tool sequence. This is not the baseline/hillclimb distinction, which controls case selection.

Read the actual assertion placement

  • Seeded-file case: it asks for the third word on the second line and requires “three” in the answer. Two expected steps and one read request are efficiency feedback, not additional hard pass conditions.
  • Overwrite case: hard checks require the resulting file to equal the new content and the answer to contain DONE.
  • Targeted-edit case: an edit_file call is expected, but the hard checks inspect the content change. A catalog title saying “prefers edit” is not enough to make tool choice a hard guarantee.

Illustratively, two runs could both produce the required /notes/report.txt, while one rereads the brief unnecessarily. They can share a correctness outcome but differ in logged efficiency. That illustrates the scoring API; it is not a recorded evaluation result.

These evaluations establish only the supplied cases and assertions under the selected model configuration. They do not prove all filesystem operations safe, all requests successful, fully grounded prose, or absence of unnecessary actions. Exact output/file assertions and judged responses have different evidence strengths.

sources.label: Hard success versus soft efficiency API
Targeted edit expectation versus content success

sections.title: The unified CLI distinguishes failures from unusable reports
sections.body:
deepagents-evals wraps single runs, repeated trials, aggregation, radar generation, catalog generation/checks, model-group discovery, and listing. It can emit JSON and preview commands.

Runner and report lifecycle

  1. Separate offline checks from real-model evaluations. The package Makefile separates offline unit tests from model evaluations. make test disables network sockets for unit tests.
  2. Choose a single run or repeated trials. make evals MODEL=... invokes the real-model suite, while make evals-trials MODEL=... TRIALS=... runs the trial aggregator. Trial summaries report variation rather than allowing a single fortunate run to stand in for stability.
  3. Derive trial failure from reports. The implementation explicitly warns that per-trial return codes are not a reliable failure signal because the reporter can rewrite pytest session status; aggregate failure is derived from report counts.
  4. Interpret the runner outcome category. Its exit taxonomy distinguishes ordinary success, evaluation failure, configuration error, and absence of usable reports.
  5. Generate and interpret reporting artifacts. Generated catalogs and model groups are checked artifacts, not hand-maintained authoritative descriptions of uninspected behavior.

Commands shown here are source-derived usage examples, not commands executed for this site.

Run them from libs/evals with a metadata-compatible Python environment, appropriate credentials, and an understood cost envelope:

# Illustrative contributor commands; not executed here.
make test
make evals MODEL=anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6
make evals-trials MODEL=anthropic:claude-sonnet-4-6 TRIALS=3
make eval-catalog
make type

A zero-exit chart-generation command proves that a chart was generated, not that its input scores were valid. Likewise, generating a catalog proves discovery, not that all cataloged evaluations passed.

sections.title: Harbor, DRBench, Context-Bench, and CLBench are separate adapters
sections.body:
The measurement-purpose map earlier separates local probes from external benchmarks. Here, compare the adapters' operating contracts: graph choice, task generation, verification, and runner environment all affect what a score means. These are independent integrations, not consecutive steps of one benchmark run.

Harbor — graph selection and environment execution

The installed LangGraph agent is extended to forward a task's skills_dir through configurable input. The benchmark project exposes dcode, bare, and tau3 graph entry points.

The factory module imports both Code and SDK construction, prepares model-specific settings, validates an absolute skill directory without .., and scrubs selected provider/tracing credentials from the shell environment. “Deep Agents benchmark” is underspecified without the selected graph entry point.

The Harbor Makefile distinguishes concurrency -n from task-count limiting -l, stages checkout dependencies, and offers Docker, Modal, Daytona, Runloop, and LangSmith environment targets.

DRBench — enterprise documents and separate verification

Tasks come from a pinned upstream commit and separately pinned container images. The adapter's app mode serves enterprise documents through Nextcloud, Mattermost, email, and a file browser. The agent environment excludes the ground-truth answer corpus; verification is designed for a separate environment after agent teardown.

No generated task directories are committed in that dataset folder. Population and deterministic-generation checks are explicit Makefile tasks. A checked-out dataset manifest does not mean every task asset is already present locally.

Context-Bench — generated self-contained tasks

Task identifiers map to indexed records in vendored filesystem JSONL. Generation copies corpus and verifier assets into self-contained Harbor tasks. The generator validates IDs as single path components before replacing a generated task directory.

CLBench — cross-response memory in an external checkout

The system adapter belongs in the external continual-learning-bench checkout. It threads an in-state memory file across responses and builds schema-specific SDK agents with structured output, rather than launching Code's host shell.

These contracts are not alternate names for one evaluation runner. Neither source commands nor checked-in scorecards establish a fresh result here. Record external models, container images, verifier behavior, credentials, and runner architecture with any reported score.
