title: Contributing and testing the actual repository
kicker: Locate the component, then choose the evidence
summary: Use package-local uv workflows and representative regression contracts, while keeping source inspection, offline tests, integration tests, evaluations, and real deployments distinct.

sections.title: Use component-local commands, not generic platform habits
sections.body:
For a first contribution, start with one component and one changed contract. You do not need to understand every provider or run every benchmark before checking a small SDK change. This checkout uses uv, local pyproject.toml/uv.lock files, Ruff, pytest, and ty, not an unrelated project's Poetry or mypy workflow.

A minimal first-contribution path

  1. Locate the owner and interpreter requirement. For a core file-tool change, work in libs/deepagents and use its package metadata. An application change instead belongs in that application's component.
  2. Sync and run the relevant offline regression. The SDK Makefile accepts TEST_FILE; selecting its file-tool test file exercises that contract without launching a paid model evaluation.
  3. Run the component's quality gate. SDK make lint checks Ruff rules and formatting, then invokes its ty type-check target. Broaden to other affected tests and integration checks according to the changed boundary.

Illustrative commands from the upstream repository root, not commands executed for this site:

cd libs/deepagents
uv sync --group test
make test TEST_FILE=tests/unit_tests/test_file_system_tools.py
make lint

Understand the wider component command map

Code and SDK Makefiles export frozen lock behavior, keep unit tests under tests/unit_tests, disable network sockets while allowing Unix sockets, and expose separate integration-test targets. Code's make check additionally checks command-catalog drift, process-current-directory discipline, imports, extras/version, lock consistency, and an advisory SDK pin.

Component working directorySource-derived commandsImportant scope
libs/deepagentsmake test, make integration_test, make lint, make typeCore offline tests; separate integration suite; ty checks package.
libs/codemake bootstrap, make check, make test TEST_FILE=...Application checks include generated catalogs and host-CWD discipline.
libs/acpmake test, make lint, make typeDefault tests folder includes protocol and unit subfolders.
libs/talonmake test, make test_bridge, make typeTest target first runs Node's WhatsApp bridge tests.
libs/evalsmake test, make evals MODEL=...Offline harness tests differ from paid/credentialed model runs.

These choose future checks; they are not reported verification. Respect package Python requirements first. The umbrella libs Makefile has a Python-version helper/comment that differs from current Code/Talon/evals metadata. Per-package metadata is stronger evidence than a claim that everything supports 3.12.

sections.title: Regression tests encode narrow, valuable contracts
sections.body:
The application test map mirrors actual boundaries. The source atlas is the path-level index for those suites.

Read the suites by application boundary

  1. Code owns application and presentation checks. Code has unit/integration suites and smoke snapshots; snapshot updates are an explicit target rather than automatic acceptance of new output.
  2. Talon covers channels, persistence, and host authority. Talon has channel-specific tests, cron tests, broad runtime/host tests, unit tests for history, embeddings, pairing, OAuth, skills, background execution, and protected approvals, plus integration adapters.
  3. ACP and partners cover protocol and adapter contracts. ACP tests concentrate on protocol behavior, multimodal conversion, model switching, local context, and execution permission reuse. Partners each retain their own adapter tests.

What inspected regressions establish

Two inspected regression examples show the kind of evidence worth carrying forward.

  1. Distinguish exact-request permission reuse. ACP tests assert that changing a command or its context requires another permission request and that identical canonical arguments can reuse a grant.
  2. Test trusted authority propagation. Talon tests exercise forged route metadata and prove the expected request metadata remains non-operator; scheduled and background delivery paths are expected to have no approval or authorization handler. These assertions target authority propagation, not just happy-path string output.

The cited source tests were inspected, not executed for this learning site. Those tests do not prove that a real Slack workspace, OAuth server, database cluster, or sandbox provider is configured correctly.

Offline fixtures can prove host routing and failure handling while missing provider behavior, account permissions, network restrictions, and deployment-specific races.

When adding a capability, identify the layer where a contract changes: tool schema, graph state, middleware routing, provider adapter, host authority, persistence, or presentation. Then update tests at that boundary rather than relying on a single end-to-end model answer.

sections.title: Read the implementation before trusting an architectural label
sections.body:
The reusable lint workflow receives a component working directory and Python version, checks out the repository, installs via the local uv setup action, runs uv sync --group test, then make lint.

  1. Keep CI scope explicit. Package-local commands are part of the CI contract. A green lint job is not a green unit-test job; a model-eval score is not a sandbox-isolation audit; a runnable example is not a production deployment. Keep those evidence categories separate when reviewing a change or interpreting a release.
  2. Read the revision and trace evidence correctly. This explorer is pinned to one source revision. Its traces are implementation-derived explanations, not recordings of executed provider calls. Source and test citations tell you where a claim comes from; they do not imply the cited test passed in this environment.
  3. Prefer implementation when introductory prose diverges. Openwiki, READMEs, and example comments can help orient a reader, but implementation wins when they diverge: current Code entrypoint names, NVIDIA's actual backend factory, and Talon's no-model echo path are concrete examples of that rule.

Debug from identity to external effect

  1. Establish the loaded package. Establish package, import, and version.
  2. Inspect effective policy. Inspect resolved configuration and trusted context.
  3. Locate the active execution owner. Locate the active process, thread, or conversation.
  4. Trace the tool boundary. Identify the tool's backend or remote bridge.
  5. Separate state lifetimes. Inspect checkpoint state, archive state, and live-task state separately.
  6. Check the actual outcome. Finally, check the observed external effect.

This order avoids blaming the model for a stale workspace binding or treating a reassuring transcript as proof of a completed write.

It also makes new contributions easier to review: describe which owner changes and which exact contract the tests establish.
